versions.text:
For fifty years the cricket pavilion at Askerby sat at the bottom of the village field, a few yards from the river Lume: a plain timber building of 1911, with a veranda, two changing rooms and a tea room. In March 1962 a gale tore away half its roof. The committee met in April, and the secretary, Moira Callan, wrote down nearly every word.

The first thing discussed was the river. In 1947 the Lume had lain a foot deep in the changing rooms for three days, and when it drained away the pavilion was still square on its footings, hardly a board sprung. The building, members told one another, had survived worse. Money was a separate worry. The club had been in debt since 1958, when a new scoreboard cost twice what Harlan Dace, the builder, had quoted, and rot was already in its posts.

Dace came with an offer. He worked mostly in brick, he said, but the timber was worth forty pounds to him if the club would sell. Tobias Fenn, the groundsman, remarked that forty pounds would pay for moving the scoreboard to higher ground. Then the captain, Neil Pryor, took a stand. He had climbed into the roof with a lamp that morning: the rafters were sound, the gale had taken only the sheeting, and the members could repair it themselves for the price of a summer's teas.

The vote was eleven to two for Pryor's plan. Through May the members worked on Saturdays, and Agnes Rowe, the headmistress, let them use the village school hall on weekday evenings to cut and paint the new boards. By June the roof was whole again, on the same building and the same footings, a few yards from the same river.

The roof those members nailed down is still on the pavilion, sixty years and many gales later. Anyone who sits on its veranda on a match day is sitting under the work of a village that looked hard at its own building, trusted what it found, and was proved right.

For fifty years the cricket pavilion at Askerby sat at the bottom of the village field, a few yards from the river Lume: a plain timber building of 1911, with a veranda, two changing rooms and a tea room. In March 1962 a gale tore away half its roof. The committee met in April, and the secretary, Moira Callan, wrote down nearly every word.

The first thing discussed was the river. In 1947 the Lume had lain a foot deep in the changing rooms for three days, and Tobias Fenn, the groundsman, had spent the following week shovelling silt out of them with two younger members. He had distrusted the site ever since. Money was a separate worry. The club had been in debt since 1958, when a new scoreboard cost twice what Harlan Dace, the builder, had quoted, and rot was already in its posts.

Dace came with an offer. He worked mostly in brick, he said, but the timber was worth forty pounds to him if the club would sell. Then Fenn rose with a plan of his own. At the north end of the field, where the ground climbed toward a stand of beeches, the pavilion could be jacked up, set on rollers and hauled to higher ground.

The captain, Neil Pryor, argued that the gale's damage was only to the sheeting and could be repaired where it stood, but the vote went nine to four for Fenn's plan, and both of his shovelling partners were among the nine. Dace was paid to do the hauling, which took six weeks instead of two and cracked the floor in two places. Agnes Rowe, the headmistress, let the club use the village school hall for the rest of the season.

The Lume has kept to its banks every year since. The pavilion sits up among the beeches, on a floor that still tilts. Reading the minutes, it is hard to escape the sense that the committee spent its savings fleeing a river that had visited once in thirty-five years, and that the club went on paying for one frightened week long after the water had gone.

For fifty years the cricket pavilion at Askerby sat at the bottom of the village field, a few yards from the river Lume: a plain timber building of 1911, with a veranda, two changing rooms and a tea room. In March 1962 a gale tore away half its roof. The committee met in April, and the secretary, Moira Callan, wrote down nearly every word.

The first thing discussed was the river. In 1947 the Lume had lain a foot deep in the changing rooms for three days, and the new floor laid afterwards had been bought on credit from Harlan Dace, the builder. The club had been in debt to him ever since. Tobias Fenn, the groundsman, had other worries: rot was in the scoreboard's posts, and he wanted the scoreboard moved to higher ground.

Dace came with an offer. He worked mostly in brick, he said, but he would pay sixty pounds for the damaged pavilion as it was, cancel the debt, and cart the whole building off to his yard in the lower village for a barn. He had run a lemonade stand at every home match for years and knew the club's accounts nearly as well as the secretary did. The captain, Neil Pryor, wanted the roof repaired where it stood, but he had no figure to set beside Dace's.

The vote was ten to three for the offer. That spring, the minutes show, the subscriptions had come to less than the interest. In July Dace's men took the pavilion apart in numbered sections and carted it away, and the teas moved to a trestle table under the scoreboard by the river. Agnes Rowe, the headmistress, let the cricketers use the village school hall for changing.

The barn is still in Dace's old yard, its veranda boarded in, and on a clear evening the faded letters ASKERBY C.C. can be made out above the door. The minutes for July 1962 give it a single line: "Pavilion removed." Old members who remember it talk mostly about teas on that veranda, and about the light going off the river from its top step on summer evenings long ago.

For fifty years the cricket pavilion at Askerby sat at the bottom of the village field, a few yards from the river Lume: a plain timber building of 1911, with a veranda, two changing rooms and a tea room. In March 1962 a gale tore away half its roof. The committee met in April, and the secretary, Moira Callan, wrote down nearly every word.

The first thing discussed was the river. In 1947 the Lume had lain a foot deep in the changing rooms for three days, and the lower wall boards had stayed damp through the following winter. Rot had started in them then, and by 1962 it had climbed into the corner posts. Money was a separate worry. The club had been in debt since 1958, when a new scoreboard cost twice what Harlan Dace, the builder, had quoted.

Dace came with an offer. He worked mostly in brick, he said, but the timber was worth forty pounds to him if the club would sell. The captain, Neil Pryor, held that the gale's damage was only to the sheeting and could be repaired where it stood. Then Moira Callan read out the county's reply to a letter she had sent in March: a sports grant would cover most of a brick pavilion on the old footings, and the wooden stand beside it, which seated eighty spectators, could come down at the same time.

The vote was eight to five for Callan's plan. Dace's men pulled the old building down in June, while Tobias Fenn, the groundsman, moved the heavy roller to higher ground. Agnes Rowe, the headmistress, let the club use the village school hall on Saturdays that season. The new pavilion, of red brick, opened the following May, and the club spent nine years paying the four hundred pounds the grant left over.

The brick pavilion is still in use at the bottom of the field, by the river. Its changing rooms were enlarged in 1988, and the tea room was fitted with a new kitchen in 2004. The minutes book records the opening match in May 1963, against Hollin Cross, and lists the eleven Askerby players by name.

For fifty years the cricket pavilion at Askerby sat at the bottom of the village field, a few yards from the river Lume: a plain timber building of 1911, with a veranda, two changing rooms and a tea room. In March 1962 a gale tore away half its roof. The committee met in April, and the secretary, Moira Callan, wrote down nearly every word.

The first thing discussed was the river. In 1947 the Lume had lain a foot deep in the changing rooms for three days, and further down the lane it had done worse, carrying off the hall of the village school. The school had made do without one ever since. Money was a separate worry. The club had been in debt since 1958, when a new scoreboard cost twice what Harlan Dace, the builder, had quoted, and rot was already in its posts.

Dace came with an offer. He worked mostly in brick, he said, but the timber was worth forty pounds to him if the club would sell. Then Agnes Rowe, the headmistress, made a proposal of her own. The club played on Saturdays, and her pupils needed a hall for the rest of the week. If the club would give the pavilion to the school, the parish would pay to carry it down the lane and repair the damaged roof. She had picked a place on the veranda for the school bell, which had hung on an iron stand in the lost hall.

Neil Pryor, the captain, wanted the roof repaired where it stood, and the vote went seven to six against him. Tobias Fenn, the groundsman, spent the summer moving the scoreboard to higher ground. In August the pavilion went down the lane toward the river on Dace's lorry, and by October it was the school hall.

Sixty years on, the cricketers walk down the lane on Saturdays to take tea among the children's paintings, and the captain rings the school bell to call them back to the field. The club that once owned the building now borrows the key from the headmistress, and the minutes record, without comment, that it has twice been late returning it.
